specPoints.text: describe the reactions of aqueous solutions of carboxylic acids with metals and metal carbonates

primer.text: From Carboxylic Acids you already know the -COOH group that ends every member of the family. This note watches that group behave like any other acid: metals and carbonates go in, and salts with a telling name ending come out.

lessons.title: Acid behaviour with metals and carbonates
lessons.opening: Diluted in water, the carboxylic acids behave like other acids you have met. Metals hand over a salt plus hydrogen, carbonates hand over a salt plus water plus carbon dioxide, and every salt name ends in anoate. This lesson pins the two patterns down.
keyPoints: Aqueous solutions of carboxylic acids react with metals to give a salt and hydrogen.
They react with metal carbonates to give a salt, water and carbon dioxide.
Salts made from these acids all end in anoate.
Methanoic acid therefore forms methanoate salts and ethanoic acid forms ethanoate salts.
The reaction with a metal produces hydrogen gas alongside the metal salt.

low.restatement: These acids react like other acids: metals give a salt plus hydrogen, and carbonates give a salt plus water plus carbon dioxide. The salt name always ends in anoate.
low.analogy: The acid group is a stamp that presses the same two patterns onto every visitor: metals leave hydrogen behind, carbonates fizz out carbon dioxide, and both leave a salt named anoate.
low.examPointer: List the products in the asked order; carbonate reactions must include water as well as the gas.

medium.restatement: Aqueous solutions of the acids attack reactive metals, releasing hydrogen and leaving a metal salt, while carbonates yield the salt, water and carbon dioxide gas. Naming follows the acid: methanoic acid gives methanoate salts, ethanoic acid gives ethanoate salts, and so on down the family.
medium.analogy: Think of the -COOH group as a fixed shop counter: metal customers pay in hydrogen, carbonate customers pay in bubbles of carbon dioxide and a splash of water, and every receipt is printed ending anoate.
medium.examPointer: Expect a follow-up asking you to name the salt, so practise converting oic acid to anoate in your head.

check.stem: What forms when an aqueous carboxylic acid reacts with a reactive metal?

options.explanation: Metals displace hydrogen from the acid, leaving the metal salt behind.
Carbon dioxide belongs to the carbonate pattern, not to metals.
Water pairs with carbonates; the metal route releases hydrogen instead.
Ester-making needs an alcohol, which plays no part here.

check.stem: Which set of products comes from a carboxylic acid plus a metal carbonate?

options.text: A salt, water and carbon dioxide
options.explanation: The carbonate supplies the carbon that leaves as the gas, and water forms alongside.
That pair is the metal pattern; carbonates never release hydrogen.
No oxygen gas is released in either pattern.
Ester-making needs an acid catalyst and an alcohol, not a carbonate.

check.stem: How do the names of salts from carboxylic acids always end?

options.explanation: The oic acid ending converts to anoate when the acid becomes a salt.
The ide ending belongs to simple salts such as sodium chloride.
The oic acid ending marks the unreacted acid, not its salts.
The yl ending belongs to the alcohol part of ester names.

check.stem: Ethanoic acid reacts with magnesium. Which salt forms?

options.explanation: The metal name fronts the anoate ending taken from ethanoic acid.
The ide ending is never used for these salts.
Methanoate salts trace back to methanoic acid, a one-carbon member.
The acid group survives inside the salt; only its hydrogen is replaced.

check.stem: Butanoic acid reacts with potassium carbonate. What is the salt called?

options.explanation: The metal supplies the first word and the four-carbon acid supplies the anoate ending.
The anoate ending is the fixed rule for this family.
Ethanoate traces back to the two-carbon acid, not the four-carbon one.
That is the reactant; the reaction consumes it and builds a new salt.

lessons.title: Example equations for ethanoate and butanoate salts
lessons.opening: Two worked patterns carry the whole topic. Ethanoic acid meeting magnesium delivers magnesium ethanoate and hydrogen gas, while butanoic acid meeting potassium carbonate fizzes out carbon dioxide and leaves potassium butanoate. This lesson reads both equations symbol by symbol.
keyPoints: Ethanoic acid plus magnesium gives magnesium ethanoate and hydrogen gas.
The equation is written 2CH3COOH + Mg giving (CH3COO)2Mg + H2.
Butanoic acid plus potassium carbonate gives potassium butanoate, water and carbon dioxide.
Balancing needs two acid molecules so the metal ion is satisfied twice.

low.restatement: Two equations show the patterns. Magnesium and ethanoic acid make magnesium ethanoate plus hydrogen. Potassium carbonate and butanoic acid make potassium butanoate plus water plus carbon dioxide.
low.analogy: Each equation is a till receipt: acid molecules enter on the left, the metal and its salt headline the right, and the gas or hydrogen is the small change.
low.examPointer: Check the balancing first in any written answer; two acids per metal ion is the pattern both equations share.

medium.restatement: With magnesium, two molecules of ethanoic acid surrender their acidic hydrogens to give (CH3COO)2Mg and H2. With potassium carbonate, two molecules of butanoic acid give 2CH3CH2CH2COOK plus water plus carbon dioxide, the gas that betrays the carbonate.
medium.analogy: Both reactions are two-door doorways: the metal or carbonate walks in one door, two acid molecules queue in the other, and the gas exits through the skylight.
medium.examPointer: Practise writing (CH3COO)2Mg with its bracket and subscript; losing the bracket is a common script slip.

check.stem: In the equation 2CH3COOH + Mg gives (CH3COO)2Mg + H2, why are two acid molecules needed?

options.text: The magnesium ion needs two ethanoate groups to balance its charge
options.explanation: Magnesium carries a 2+ charge, so two singly-charged ethanoate ions partner it.

options.text: One acid molecule is too heavy to react alone
options.explanation: Mass has nothing to do with it; charge balance drives the ratio.

options.text: Hydrogen only forms when acid is in excess
options.explanation: Hydrogen forms whatever the amount; the ratio is set by charges.

options.text: The second molecule acts as a catalyst
options.explanation: Neither acid molecule is recovered unchanged, so neither is a catalyst.

check.stem: Which observation confirms the carbonate reaction of a carboxylic acid?

options.text: Fizzing as carbon dioxide is released
options.explanation: The carbonate pattern always releases the gas, which shows as effervescence.

options.text: A colour change from orange to green
options.explanation: That observation belongs to dichromate oxidations, not carbonates.

options.text: A smarting smell of the ester forming
options.explanation: No ester forms when a carbonate meets the acid.

options.text: A blue flame appearing above the mixture
options.explanation: Nothing burns in an acid-carbonate mixture.

check.stem: Which formula is magnesium ethanoate written correctly?

options.explanation: The bracket doubles the ethanoate group onto the single magnesium ion.
Without the bracket the charges do not balance.
The methyl part of the group has been lost entirely.
The subscript sits on the wrong side; two groups partner one metal.

check.stem: What does the gas tested in the carbonate reaction turn limewater into?

options.text: It turns limewater milky, proving carbon dioxide
options.explanation: The cloudy limewater test is the standard proof for carbon dioxide.

options.text: It burns with a squeaky pop, proving hydrogen
options.explanation: The pop test identifies hydrogen, which carbonates do not release here.

options.text: It relights a glowing splint, proving oxygen
options.explanation: Oxygen is not among the products of an acid-carbonate reaction.

options.text: It bleaches damp litmus, proving chlorine
options.explanation: Chlorine plays no part in this reaction.

check.stem: In the butanoic acid equation, what does COOK at the end of CH3CH2CH2COOK represent?

options.text: The potassium ion taking the place of the acidic hydrogen
options.explanation: Metals replace the acid hydrogen to build the salt, so K closes the chain.

options.text: A cooking abbreviation left in the formula
options.explanation: The letters are element symbols: carbon, oxygen, potassium.
The salt is a solid dissolved in water, not a gas.

options.text: An unreacted piece of the carbonate
options.explanation: The carbonate has been broken apart; potassium now sits in the salt.

glossary.definition: The ionic compound left behind when the acidic hydrogen of an acid is replaced by a metal.
A compound of a metal with carbonate ions that fizzes with acids to release carbon dioxide.
The salt form of ethanoic acid; its names end in anoate, as in magnesium ethanoate.
The fizzing seen when a gas escapes from a reacting mixture, as here with carbon dioxide.
The standard check for carbon dioxide, which turns limewater cloudy or milky.

workedExample.prompt: a) Write the equation for ethanoic acid reacting with magnesium and name the salt. b) Write the equation for butanoic acid reacting with potassium carbonate and name the salt. c) Why are two molecules of acid needed in each equation?
steps: a) 2CH3COOH + Mg → (CH3COO)2Mg + H2 — carboxylic acid + metal gives salt + hydrogen; the salt is magnesium ethanoate.
b) 2CH3CH2CH2COOH + K2CO3 → 2CH3CH2CH2COOK + H2O + CO2 — carboxylic acid + carbonate gives salt + water + carbon dioxide (seen as fizzing); the salt is potassium butanoate.
c) Two acid molecules supply the two anions needed to satisfy the metal ion's charge — one ethanoate (or butanoate) ion per unit of positive charge; salts of these acids always end in -anoate.
workedExample.finalAnswer: a) 2CH3COOH + Mg → (CH3COO)2Mg + H2 (magnesium ethanoate). b) 2CH3CH2CH2COOH + K2CO3 → 2CH3CH2CH2COOK + H2O + CO2 (potassium butanoate). c) Two acid molecules give the two anions the metal ions require.
